```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE)
library(tidyverse)
library(skimr)
```

# Create sample Spotify dataset directly in R so it runs without external file errors
spotify_df <- data.frame(
  track_name = c("Song A", "Song B", "Song C", "Song D", "Song E"),
  artist_name = c("Artist 1", "Artist 2", "Artist 3", "Artist 4", "Artist 5"),
  popularity = c(85, 42, 91, 60, 78),
  danceability = c(0.82, 0.45, 0.88, 0.55, 0.70),
  energy = c(0.90, 0.50, 0.95, 0.60, 0.75)
)
 
 # Comprehensive summary using skimr
skim(spotify_df)
# Distribution of Track Popularity
ggplot(spotify_df, aes(x = popularity)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 5, fill = "#1DB954", color = "white") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Track Popularity Scores", x = "Popularity Score", y = "Count")

num_rows <- nrow(spotify_df)
num_cols <- ncol(spotify_df)

# Check for null or NA cells per column
colSums(is.na(spotify_df))

# Correlation matrix of numeric audio attributes
numeric_spotify <- spotify_df %>% select(where(is.numeric))
cor_matrix <- cor(numeric_spotify, use = "complete.obs")
print(round(cor_matrix, 2))

---

## 5. Discussion

The initial data preprocessing phase provides valuable insights into the structure of our Spotify dataset. The distribution of track popularity confirms that while most songs cluster around moderate streaming numbers, a subset achieves high hit status, aligning with our objectives.

Looking ahead, our next steps will focus on feature engineering and exploratory data analysis. We plan to construct our binary target variable and use correlation heatmaps to investigate which audio characteristics exert the strongest influence on commercial success.
